# Sand and loam moulding for large castings (`sand_loam_casting`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: helped by copper_bronze, blast_furnace_cast_iron, lost_wax_casting
- Core idea: For repeated castings, ram damp sand with a little clay round a wooden pattern in a two-part box, lift the halves apart, take the pattern out, cut a pouring channel and risers, and close the box again; a baked sand core makes a hollow. The pattern is reused. For large round things (bells, cannon, pots, engine cylinders) build the mould in loam, a paste of clay, sand and horse dung or chopped straw, struck to shape with a profile board turning on a spindle: first the core, then a false layer the thickness of the metal, then the outer cope; take the false layer out, dry everything by fire and bury the mould in a pit to resist the pressure. Metal shrinks on cooling (cast iron about 1 %, bronze 1.5 %), so patterns are made oversize and risers feed the shrinking casting.
- Pitfalls:
  - Wet moulds or a damp pit: steam explosions with molten metal
  - No allowance for shrinkage, and no risers, so the casting is undersize and has cavities
  - A core that floats up in the heavy liquid metal unless anchored
  - Sharp inside corners and sudden changes of thickness, where castings crack as they cool
- History: mesopotamia: 4th millennium BC – open stone and clay moulds; china: c. 1600–1050 BC – Shang ritual bronzes cast in sectional ceramic piece-moulds; 5th–3rd c. BC cast-iron tools made in stacked and in iron permanent moulds; india: c. 400 AD and later – large iron and bronze founding; c. 1000 Chola bronzes (lost wax); europe: c. 1122 – Theophilus on bell founding in loam; 1540 Biringuccio on cannon and bells; 1707 Abraham Darby's patent for casting iron pots in sand; 1720s loam-moulded iron engine cylinders at Coalbrookdale
- Read:
  - Theophilus, On Divers Arts (c. 1122; tr. J. G. Hawthorne & C. S. Smith, 1963)
  - Vannoccio Biringuccio, De la pirotechnia (1540; tr. C. S. Smith & M. T. Gnudi, 1942)
